newsitem.title: DENMARK: SAS lags in filling aircraft seats.
newsitem.headline: SAS lags in filling aircraft seats.

text.p: Comparisons with figures published by some other European airlines shows Scandinavian Airlines System (SAS) lagging behind in the percentage of available aircraft seats filled.

SAS on Monday reported a 31 percent fall in 1996 pre-tax profits to 1.82 billion Swedish crowns ($246 million) and said that the number of seats filled fell by 1.5 percent over the year to an average 63.5 percent of capacity.
The figure for the last quarter of 1996 was 61.1 percent, a spokesman said on Tuesday.

Rival British Airways, whose reporting year runs from April to March logged a record cabin load factor of 71.2 percent during the last three months of 1996, up from 70.7 percent over the same period the year before.
Dutch carrier KLM, which also has an April-March accounting year, said it filled 71.5 percent of available seats in December 1996, compared to 69.1 percent in December 1995.
In its report SAS said it had more seats on offer in 1996 but that the number of passengers to fill them had not grown at the same rate.
"SAS regards this development seriously and will make an effort to attract the private travel market, in order to better exploit vacant seat capacity," it said.

Directly comparable figures were not available, but KLM said that over the nine months to December 31, 1996 it increased the number of seat/kilometres available by about eight percent while raising capacity utilisation by one percent over the same period.
SAS, jointly owned by the governments of Denmark, Norway and Sweden and private investors, forecast that competition would increase available capacity still more in 1997.

"Competition in the airline industry is expected...to intensify further in 1997 which could lead to big over-capacity, putting pressure on prices and revenue," SAS said in a statement accompanying Monday's report. --Steve Weizman, Copenhagen newsroom +45 33969650
